title: French grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday French, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is French as it is spoken in France today.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name, your nationality and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first French conversation.
lessons.topic: {{je m'appelle}} “my name is”, {{je suis}} “I am”; nationalities for a man and a woman; {{et vous ?}}

goal.t: Bonjour, je m'appelle Emma. Je suis américaine.
goal.tr: Hello, my name is Emma. I'm American.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Lyon.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, it.

blocks.p: **Saying who you are.** {{Je m'appelle…}} is “my name is…” (word for word, “I call myself…”). {{Je suis…}} is “I am…”: {{je suis américaine}} “I'm American”, {{je suis de Lyon}} “I'm from Lyon”. {{De}} is “from”.

**I is je.** “I” is {{je}}, with a small letter (English “I” is always a capital; French {{je}} isn't). Before a vowel, the {{e}} drops and an apostrophe takes its place: {{je m'appelle}} is {{je}} + {{me}} “myself” + {{appelle}}.

**Men and women.** Words that say what someone is often change for a woman. Usually you add {{-e}}: Emma says {{je suis américaine}}; Thomas would say {{je suis américain}}. When the word ends in a consonant, the {{-e}} makes you hear it: {{français}} ends in a silent {{s}}, but in {{française}} you hear a “z” sound.
**And you?** {{Et vous ?}} turns the question back to the other person. {{Vous}} is the polite “you”, for someone you don't know yet. The next lesson shows the friendly one, {{tu}}.

ex.note: no word for “a” before a job (lesson 4)
to a woman: a question just by raising your voice
adding {{monsieur}} or {{madame}} is polite, not stiff

blocks.tip: Nationalities take a small letter in French: {{je suis anglais}}. Say {{bonjour}} all day, and {{bonsoir}} “good evening” from about six o'clock.

mistakes.why: {{Je m'appelle}} already means “my name is”: there is no “is” to add.

lessons.title: Ask how someone is, politely or as a friend
lessons.summary: Ask “How are you?” and answer it, choosing {{tu}} for a friend and {{vous}} for everyone else.
lessons.topic: {{tu}} or {{vous}}; {{ça va}}, {{comment allez-vous}}; {{moi}}, {{toi}}

goal.t: Salut, ça va ? — Ça va bien, et toi ?
goal.tr: Hi, how are you? — I'm fine, and you?

dialog.t: Salut, Hugo ! Ça va ?
dialog.tr: Hi, Hugo! How's it going?

dialog.t: Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: Fine, thanks. And you?

dialog.t: Bof, je suis fatiguée.
dialog.tr: Meh, I'm tired.

dialog.t: Moi aussi !
dialog.tr: Me too!

blocks.p: **Two ways to say “you”.** Léa and Hugo are friends, so they say {{tu}} to each other ({{toi}} when the word stands alone: {{et toi ?}}). With someone you don't know, French uses {{vous}}. The greeting changes with it.

dialog.t: Bonjour, monsieur Dubois. Comment allez-vous ?
dialog.tr: Hello, Mr. Dubois. How are you?

dialog.t: Très bien, merci. Et vous ?
dialog.tr: Very well, thank you. And you?

dialog.t: Bien, merci.
dialog.tr: Fine, thanks.

blocks.means: polite and careful, for people you don't know well, older people, at work. Its opposite is informal: relaxed, for friends and family.

table: a friend, family, a child, a pet
someone you don't know, an older person, a colleague, a shop assistant

blocks.p: When in doubt, say {{vous}}: it is never rude. Young people switch to {{tu}} with each other at once; with anyone else, wait until they ask {{On peut se tutoyer ?}} “Shall we say tu?”. And {{vous}} is also “you” to several people, friends or not: {{Vous allez bien, les enfants ?}} “Are you all right, kids?”.

**Moi, toi.** {{Moi}} “me” and {{toi}} “you” are the forms that stand alone: {{Et toi ?}}, {{Moi aussi.}} “Me too.” The French also put {{moi}} in front of {{je}} to say “as for me”: {{Moi, je suis fatigué.}}

ex.note: {{ça va}} is both the question and the answer
word for word “I go very well”

blocks.tip: Answers to {{Ça va ?}}, from good to bad: {{Très bien !}}, {{Ça va bien.}}, {{Ça va.}}, {{Pas mal.}}, {{Bof.}}, {{Pas terrible.}} The French really do say {{bof}} when things are just so-so.

mistakes.why: Standing alone, “you” is {{toi}} (or {{vous}}), never {{tu}}.
To say how you are, French uses “go”: {{je vais bien}}. {{Je suis bien}} means “I'm comfortable”.
{{Salut}} is for friends. To someone you call {{madame}}, say {{bonjour}} and {{vous}}.

lessons.title: Ask for things politely
lessons.summary: Order a coffee, buy a ticket, ask for a room: {{je voudrais}}, and the first thing to know about French nouns, their gender.
lessons.topic: {{je voudrais}} + {{un}} or {{une}}; masculine and feminine nouns

goal.t: Je voudrais un café et une baguette, s'il vous plaît.
goal.tr: I'd like a coffee and a baguette, please.

dialog.t: Bonjour, madame. Vous désirez ?
dialog.tr: Hello, madam. What would you like?

dialog.t: Bonjour. Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
dialog.tr: Hello. I'd like a coffee, please.

dialog.t: Un café. Et avec ça ?
dialog.tr: One coffee. Anything else?

dialog.t: Et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
dialog.tr: And a croissant, please.

dialog.t: Très bien, madame.
dialog.tr: Very good, madam.

blocks.p: **Asking politely.** {{Je voudrais}} is “I would like”. It is the polite way to ask for anything, in a café, a shop, a hotel or a station: {{je voudrais}}, the thing you want, then {{s'il vous plaît}}.

blocks.means: a word for a thing, a person, a place or an idea: coffee, ticket, friend, Paris, love.
in French, every noun is either masculine or feminine, things included: {{café}} is masculine, {{baguette}} is feminine. That is the noun's gender.
a little word in front of a noun: “a” and “the” in English. In French it also shows the noun's gender: {{un}}, {{une}}.

blocks.p: **Un or une?** “A” is {{un}} before a masculine noun and {{une}} before a feminine one. The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: there's nothing feminine about a table, but it's {{une table}}.

table: {{une bouteille d'eau}} a bottle of water

blocks.p: **Learn each noun with its un or une.** There are hints (most nouns ending in {{-tion}}, {{-té}} or {{-ette}} are feminine; most ending in {{-ment}} or {{-eau}} are masculine), but the surest way is to learn {{une chambre}}, not just {{chambre}}.

ex.t: Je voudrais un thé, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais une chambre pour deux nuits.
ex.tr: I'd like a room for two nights.

ex.t: Je voudrais un billet pour Paris.
ex.tr: I'd like a ticket to Paris.
I'd like a bottle of water.

ex.note: short, and fine at a counter

ex.t: Je voudrais l'addition, s'il vous plaît.
ex.tr: Could I have the check, please?

blocks.tip: {{Un}} and {{une}} also mean “one”: {{un café}} is “a coffee” or “one coffee”, {{une nuit}} “one night”.

mistakes.right: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend, say where people are from and what they do: all of {{être}} “to be”.
lessons.topic: {{être}}: {{je suis, tu es, il est…}}; {{il}}, {{elle}}, {{ils}}, {{elles}}; jobs without “a”; {{c'est}} or {{il est}}

goal.t: Voici Marc. C'est mon ami. Il est médecin.
goal.tr: This is Marc. He's my friend. He's a doctor.

dialog.t: Paul, voici Marc et Sophie. Ils sont de Bordeaux.
dialog.tr: Paul, this is Marc and Sophie. They're from Bordeaux.

dialog.t: Bonjour ! Vous êtes en vacances ?
dialog.tr: Hello! Are you on vacation?

dialog.t: Non, nous sommes ici pour le travail. Je suis infirmière et Marc est médecin.
dialog.tr: No, we're here for work. I'm a nurse and Marc is a doctor.

dialog.t: Ah, c'est super !
dialog.tr: Oh, that's great!

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, have, be.
who or what the sentence is about, usually just before the verb: **Marc** is a doctor; **we** are here.
to give a verb the form that goes with its subject: {{je suis}}, {{tu es}}, {{il est}}. All these forms together are the verb's conjugation.

blocks.p: **One verb, many forms.** “To be” is {{être}}. Like most French verbs, it changes with its subject. English does this a little (I am, he is); French has a form for almost every person.
**He, she, they.** {{Il}} is “he”, {{elle}} is “she”. For “they”, French chooses too: {{elles}} for a group of women only, {{ils}} for men, and for any mixed group (even one man among ten women).

**Jobs without “a”.** After {{je suis}}, {{il est}} and the rest, a job has no article: {{Il est médecin.}} “He's a doctor.” Like nationalities, many jobs change for a woman: {{étudiant}}, {{étudiante}}; {{infirmier}}, {{infirmière}}.

**C'est or il est?** To present someone, use {{c'est}} “this is, he is, she is” before a name, or before a noun with its article: {{C'est Marc.}} {{C'est mon ami.}} {{C'est un bon médecin.}} Use {{il est}} or {{elle est}} before a job, a nationality or a description standing alone: {{Il est médecin.}} {{Elle est sympa.}}

ex.tr: This is Sophie. She's a nurse.

blocks.tip: {{Vous êtes}} is said “voo-zet”: the {{s}} at the end of {{vous}}, normally silent, is heard as a “z” before a vowel. This joining is called liaison. The {{t}} in {{c'est un}} does it too: “say-tun”.

mistakes.why: After {{il est}}, a job has no {{un}} or {{une}}. (With {{c'est}} it needs one: {{C'est un médecin.}})

lessons.title: Say what you have, your age and how you feel
lessons.summary: Talk about your family, say how old you are and that you're hungry or cold: with {{avoir}} “to have”, where English says “be”.
lessons.topic: {{avoir}}: {{j'ai, tu as, il a…}}; {{j'ai 30 ans}}; {{j'ai faim}}, {{j'ai froid}}

goal.t: J'ai trente ans et j'ai deux enfants.
goal.tr: I'm thirty and I have two children.

dialog.t: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
dialog.tr: Do you have brothers and sisters?

dialog.t: Oui, j'ai une sœur. Elle a vingt ans.
dialog.tr: Yes, I have a sister. She's twenty.

dialog.t: Et toi, tu as quel âge ?
dialog.tr: And how old are you?

dialog.t: J'ai vingt-cinq ans.
dialog.tr: I'm twenty-five.

dialog.t: Moi aussi ! Tu as faim ?
dialog.tr: Me too! Are you hungry?

dialog.t: Oui, j'ai très faim !
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm really hungry!

blocks.p: **Having.** {{Avoir}} is “to have”. Like {{être}}, it changes with its subject. With {{je}}, it's {{j'ai}}: {{je}} loses its {{e}} before a vowel.
Listen for the difference between {{ils ont}} “they have” and {{ils sont}} “they are”: in {{ils ont}} you hear a “z” (“eel-zon”), in {{ils sont}} an “s” (“eel-son”).

**Your age is something you have.** French says “I have thirty years”: {{J'ai trente ans.}} The word {{ans}} “years” is never left out. To ask: {{Tu as quel âge ?}} or, politely, {{Vous avez quel âge ?}}
**Feelings you have.** Where English says “I am hungry”, French says “I have hunger”: {{J'ai faim.}} It's the same for thirst, cold, heat, fear, sleepiness, and for being right.

ex.t: Vous avez une chambre pour ce soir ?

lessons.title: Say no and what isn't so
lessons.summary: Say what you're not, what you don't have and that you don't understand: {{ne … pas}} around the verb.
lessons.topic: {{ne … pas}}; {{n'}} before a vowel; {{pas de}} after a negative

goal.t: Pardon, je ne comprends pas.
goal.tr: Sorry, I don't understand.

dialog.t: Vous êtes anglaise ?
dialog.tr: Are you English?

dialog.t: Non, je ne suis pas anglaise, je suis américaine.
dialog.tr: No, I'm not English, I'm American.

dialog.t: Vous avez un sac ?
dialog.tr: Do you have a bag?

dialog.t: Non, je n'ai pas de sac.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have a bag.

dialog.t: Pas de problème, voilà un sac.
dialog.tr: No problem, here's a bag.

blocks.means: a sentence that says something is not so: I'm not English; I don't have a bag.

blocks.p: **Two pieces around the verb.** French puts {{ne}} before the verb and {{pas}} after it, like the bread of a sandwich: {{je suis}} → {{je ne suis pas}}. Before a vowel, {{ne}} becomes {{n'}}: {{j'ai}} → {{je n'ai pas}}.
**No “do”.** English adds “do” to say no (“I **don't** understand”). French doesn't: just {{ne … pas}} around the verb itself.

**Un and une become de.** After a negative, “a” ({{un}}, {{une}}) becomes {{de}}, or {{d'}} before a vowel: {{J'ai un sac.}} → {{Je n'ai pas de sac.}} “I don't have a bag.” But after {{être}} they stay: {{Ce n'est pas un problème.}} “It's not a problem.”

ex.t: Nous n'avons pas de chambre pour ce soir.
ex.tr: We don't have a room for tonight.

ex.note: word for word “it isn't serious”: you'll hear it every day

blocks.tip: In everyday speech the French often drop {{ne}}: {{C'est pas grave.}} {{Je sais pas.}} “I dunno.” You'll hear it everywhere. In writing, and while you learn, keep {{ne}}.

mistakes.why: {{Ne}} alone isn't enough: {{pas}} goes after the verb.
After a negative, {{un}} and {{une}} become {{de}}.
The verb goes between {{ne}} and {{pas}}.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions in three ways, and ask where, when, how, how much, who, what and why.
lessons.topic: questions with the voice, with {{est-ce que}} and with question words; {{quel}}; inversion to recognise

goal.t: Excusez-moi, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the train station, please?

dialog.t: Excusez-moi, est-ce que vous parlez anglais ?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, do you speak English?

dialog.t: Un peu. Qu'est-ce que vous cherchez ?

dialog.tr: You're welcome!

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions: three ways.** Take any sentence, {{Vous parlez anglais.}} “You speak English.”, and…

table: raise your voice at the end (everyday speech)
put {{est-ce que}} in front (everyday, a little more careful)
swap the verb and the pronoun, with a dash (formal, written)

blocks.p: The first two are what you'll say. The third, called inversion, is what you'll read, and hear in formal situations: recognise it for now. {{Est-ce que}} becomes {{est-ce qu'}} before a vowel: {{Est-ce qu'il est là ?}} “Is he here?”

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: where, when, how, who, what, why.

blocks.p: **Where the question word goes.** In everyday French it can come first, or go at the end, where the answer would be: {{Où est la gare ?}} or {{La gare est où ?}}. After a question word at the start you can add {{est-ce que}}: {{Quand est-ce que tu arrives ?}}

**Which? What?** Before a noun, “what” or “which” is {{quel}}. It changes like the words in lesson 1: {{quel}} (masculine), {{quelle}} (feminine), {{quels}}, {{quelles}} (more than one). All four sound the same: {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} “What time is it?”, {{Tu as quel âge ?}} “How old are you?”

ex.t: Où sont les toilettes, s'il vous plaît ?

ex.note: to a friend; politely: {{Comment vous appelez-vous ?}}

ex.t: Pourquoi ? — Parce que je suis fatigué.

blocks.tip: To answer “yes” to a negative question, French has a special word: {{si}}. {{Tu n'as pas faim ? — Si !}} “Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I am!” A plain {{oui}} would sound odd here.

mistakes.why: For age, ask “what age” ({{quel âge}}), with {{avoir}}.

mistakes.tr: Aren't you hungry? — Yes, I am!
mistakes.why: To say yes to a negative question, French says {{si}}.

goal.t: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — C'est une crêpe, la spécialité de la maison !
goal.tr: What's this? — It's a crêpe, the house specialty!

dialog.t: Qu'est-ce que c'est ?

blocks.p: **A or the.** As in English, “a” ({{un}}, {{une}}) is for something new, “the” for something you both know about. Sam says {{des chocolats}} “some chocolates”, then {{les chocolats}} “the chocolates”: the ones he has just mentioned.

blocks.means: more than one: books, children. One is singular.

blocks.p: **Plurals.** Most nouns add {{-s}} in the plural, as in English, but in French the {{s}} is silent: {{livre}} and {{livres}} sound the same. So you hear the plural in the article: {{le livre}} “luh”, {{les livres}} “lay”. Nouns ending in {{-eau}} add {{-x}}: {{un gâteau}}, {{des gâteaux}}.
**Des.** In the plural, English often says nothing (“They're chocolates”). French needs an article: {{Ce sont des chocolats.}}
**C'est, ce sont.** {{C'est…}} “it's, this is” for one thing, {{ce sont…}} “they're, these are” for more than one. In speech you'll often hear {{c'est}} for both.
**L'.** Before a vowel or a silent {{h}}, {{le}} and {{la}} shorten to {{l'}}: {{l'eau}} “the water”, {{l'hôtel}} “the hotel”. And {{les}} links to a vowel with a “z”: {{les amis}} “lay-zah-mee”.

ex.tr: Is this the train to Lyon?

ex.t: Ce sont des amis de Paris.

blocks.tip: Learn each noun with {{le}} or {{la}}, or {{un}} or {{une}}: {{l'}} and {{les}} hide the gender. {{L'hôtel}} doesn't tell you that hotel is masculine ({{un hôtel}}).

lessons.summary: Say what something is like, big or small, new or old, red or blue: adjectives that agree with their noun and mostly come after it.
lessons.topic: adjectives: agreement ({{-e}}, {{-s}}); after the noun, except a few short ones ({{grand, petit, bon, beau, nouveau, vieux, jeune}}…)

goal.t: C'est une petite maison blanche avec un grand jardin.
goal.tr: It's a little white house with a big yard.

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, red, French, kind.
to take the form that matches another word. A French adjective takes the gender of its noun, and its number (one or more than one).

blocks.p: **Agreement.** Add {{-e}} for a feminine noun, {{-s}} for a plural, {{-es}} for both. As with nouns, the {{-s}} is silent; the {{-e}} lets you hear a final consonant: {{noir}} and {{noire}} sound the same, but {{petit}} “puh-tee” becomes {{petite}} “puh-teet”.

An adjective that already ends in {{-e}} doesn't add another: {{un sac rouge}}, {{une valise rouge}}. Some change more: {{blanc}} → {{blanche}}, {{bon}} → {{bonne}}, {{gentil}} → {{gentille}}, {{italien}} → {{italienne}}.

**After the noun, mostly.** French usually puts the adjective after the noun: {{une voiture rouge}} “a red car”, {{un film intéressant}} “an interesting movie”. Colors and nationalities always go after.

**A few short ones go before.** About ten very common adjectives come before the noun. They're about beauty, age, goodness and size: {{beau}} (beautiful), {{joli}} (pretty), {{jeune}} (young), {{vieux}} (old), {{nouveau}} (new), {{bon}} (good), {{mauvais}} (bad), {{grand}} (big, tall), {{petit}} (small).
**With être.** After {{être}}, the adjective agrees with the subject: {{Il est petit.}} {{Elle est petite.}} {{Ils sont contents.}}

blocks.tip: {{Beau}}, {{nouveau}} and {{vieux}} have their own feminine forms: {{belle}}, {{nouvelle}}, {{vieille}}. {{Une belle journée}} “a beautiful day”, {{une vieille voiture}} “an old car”.

mistakes.why: Colors go after the noun.
{{Maison}} is feminine, so the adjective is too: {{petite}}.
After {{être}}, the adjective agrees with the subject: feminine and plural, {{-es}}.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.summary: Talk about your family and your things: “my, your, his, her” in French, and {{de}} for “Paul's”.
lessons.topic: {{mon, ma, mes}}, {{ton, ta, tes}}, {{son, sa, ses}}, {{notre, votre, leur}}; {{la voiture de Paul}}

goal.t: Voici ma sœur et son mari. Et ce sont leurs enfants.
goal.tr: This is my sister and her husband. And these are their children.

dialog.t: C'est ta famille ?
dialog.tr: Is that your family?

dialog.t: Oui ! Voici mon père et ma mère.
dialog.tr: Yes! This is my father and my mother.

dialog.t: Et le garçon, c'est ton frère ?

dialog.tr: No, it's my sister's son. His name is Léo.

dialog.t: Il est mignon !
dialog.tr: He's cute!

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is: my, your, his, her, our, their.

blocks.p: **My, your…** “My” agrees with the thing you have, like an adjective: {{mon}} before a masculine noun, {{ma}} before a feminine one, {{mes}} before a plural.

**His or her: the same word.** {{Son}}, {{sa}} and {{ses}} mean “his” or “her”. They agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: {{sa mère}} is “his mother” or “her mother”, because {{mère}} is feminine; {{son père}} is “his father” or “her father”. The rest of the sentence tells you who.

**Before a vowel: mon.** Before a feminine word that starts with a vowel, {{ma}}, {{ta}} and {{sa}} become {{mon}}, {{ton}}, {{son}}, just to sound smooth: {{mon amie}} “my friend” (a woman), {{son école}} “his school, her school”.
**Paul's: la … de Paul.** French has no 's. Say “the car of Paul”: {{la voiture de Paul}}; {{le fils de ma sœur}} “my sister's son”.

ex.note: {{frère}} is masculine, so {{son}}, though Marie is a woman

ex.t: C'est la voiture de mon père.

blocks.tip: “Your” follows “you”: {{ton, ta, tes}} with someone you call {{tu}}, {{votre, vos}} with {{vous}}. At a hotel: {{Votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?}} “Your name, please?”

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: Say what there is and where: {{il y a}} “there is, there are”, and “on, under, next to, opposite”, with {{du}} and {{au}}.
lessons.topic: {{il y a}}; {{dans, sur, sous, devant, derrière, entre, à côté de, près de, en face de}}; {{du}}, {{des}}, {{au}}, {{aux}}

goal.t: Il y a une pharmacie à côté de la gare.
goal.tr: There's a pharmacy next to the station.

dialog.t: Excusez-moi, il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a supermarket near here?

dialog.t: Oui, il y a un supermarché en face du musée.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's a supermarket opposite the museum.

dialog.t: Et il y a des restaurants dans le quartier ?

dialog.t: Oui, il y a beaucoup de restaurants à côté de la place.
dialog.tr: Yes, there are a lot of restaurants next to the square.

dialog.t: Merci !
dialog.tr: Thank you!

blocks.p: **There is, there are: il y a.** {{Il y a}} is both “there is” and “there are”: {{il y a une pharmacie}}, {{il y a des restaurants}}. To ask, raise your voice or start with {{est-ce qu'}}: {{Est-ce qu'il y a un bus ?}} To say no: {{il n'y a pas de…}}

blocks.means: a little word that shows where, when or how: on, under, in, with, to.
two words joined into one, like “do not” → “don't”. In French it isn't optional: {{de}} + {{le}} is always {{du}}.

blocks.p: **De + le = du.** The prepositions ending in {{de}} ({{à côté de}}, {{près de}}, {{en face de}}) join with {{le}} and {{les}}: {{de + le}} becomes {{du}}, {{de + les}} becomes {{des}}. With {{la}} and {{l'}}, nothing changes. {{À}} “at, in, to” joins the same way: {{au}}, {{aux}}.

ex.t: La banque est entre la poste et la pharmacie.

ex.t: Il n'y a pas de bus le dimanche.

blocks.tip: {{Il y a}} is said fast, almost “ya”: {{Y a un problème ?}} “Is there a problem?” And {{Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?}} means “What's the matter?”

mistakes.why: {{De}} + {{le}} always becomes {{du}}.
{{À}} + {{le}} always becomes {{au}}.

lessons.summary: Ask the price, understand the answer and buy the right amount: numbers to 100, {{combien}}, and {{un kilo de}}.
lessons.topic: numbers to 100 ({{soixante-dix}}, {{quatre-vingts}}); {{combien}}, {{combien de}}; amounts with {{de}}

blocks.p: **Asking the price.** {{C'est combien ?}} “How much is it?”, {{Ça coûte combien ?}} “How much does it cost?”, and at the checkout {{Ça fait combien ?}} “How much is that (all together)?”

table: {{un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix}}

blocks.p: **70, 80, 90.** From 60 on, French in France counts in twenties: 70 is “sixty-ten”, 80 “four twenties”, 90 “four twenties ten”. (In Belgium and Switzerland you'll hear {{septante}} and {{nonante}}, but not in France.)
**Prices.** The euros first, then the cents, usually without the word {{centimes}}: {{4,80 €}} is {{quatre euros quatre-vingts}}. French writes a comma where English writes a decimal point.

**How many: combien de.** Before a noun, “how much” or “how many” is {{combien de}}: {{Combien de personnes ?}} “How many people?” Amounts take {{de}} too, with no article: {{un kilo de tomates}}, {{un verre de vin}}, {{beaucoup de monde}} “a lot of people”, {{un peu de sucre}} “a little sugar”.

ex.t: C'est combien, le croissant ? — Un euro vingt.
ex.tr: How much is the croissant? — One euro twenty.

ex.t: Combien de personnes ? — Nous sommes quatre.
ex.tr: How many people? — There are four of us.

ex.t: Je voudrais deux kilos de pommes.

ex.t: Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
ex.tr: A glass of red wine, please.

ex.t: Il y a beaucoup de monde !
ex.tr: There are a lot of people!

blocks.tip: {{Six}} and {{dix}} end in an “s” sound on their own, a “z” before a vowel ({{six euros}} “see-zeuro”), and nothing before a consonant ({{six pommes}} “see pom”).

lessons.title: Say what you do: work, home, languages
lessons.summary: Say where you live, where you work and what languages you speak: the present of -er verbs (nine French verbs in ten), and {{on}} “we”.
lessons.topic: the present of -er verbs ({{parler, habiter, travailler}}); silent endings; {{on}} for “we”

goal.t: J'habite à Lyon et je travaille dans une banque.
goal.tr: I live in Lyon and I work in a bank.

dialog.t: Tu habites où ?
dialog.tr: Where do you live?

dialog.t: J'habite à Lyon, près de la gare. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: I live in Lyon, near the station. And you?

dialog.t: Moi aussi ! Tu travailles ici ?
dialog.tr: Me too! Do you work here?

dialog.t: Oui, je travaille dans une école. J'enseigne l'anglais.
dialog.tr: Yes, I work in a school. I teach English.

dialog.t: Tu parles bien français !
dialog.tr: You speak French well!

dialog.t: Merci ! Mon mari est français, alors on parle français à la maison.
dialog.tr: Thanks! My husband is French, so we speak French at home.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: “to speak”, {{parler}}. French infinitives end in {{-er}}, {{-ir}} or {{-re}}.

blocks.p: **Nine verbs in ten end in -er.** {{Parler}} “to speak”, {{habiter}} “to live”, {{travailler}} “to work”, {{aimer}} “to like”, {{regarder}} “to watch”… They all work the same way: take off {{-er}} and add the ending for each person.

**The good news: most endings are silent.** {{Parle}}, {{parles}} and {{parlent}} all sound exactly the same: “parl”. Only {{nous parlons}} and {{vous parlez}} sound different. So when you speak, an -er verb has three forms, not six.

**On, the everyday “we”.** {{On}} means “one, people”, but in speech the French use it for “we” all the time: {{On parle français.}} “We speak French.” It takes the same form as {{il}}. {{Nous}} is for writing and careful speech.

**One present for two in English.** {{Je travaille}} is both “I work” and “I'm working”: French has a single present. {{Je travaille.}} “I'm working (right now).” {{Je travaille le samedi.}} “I work on Saturdays.”

ex.t: Je parle anglais et un peu français.
ex.tr: I speak English and a little French.

ex.t: On regarde un film ce soir ?
ex.tr: Shall we watch a movie tonight?

blocks.tip: The {{-ent}} of a verb is never said: {{ils travaillent}} is “eel tra-vye”. But at the end of other words you do hear it, as a nasal “ahn”: {{souvent}} “often”, {{content}} “happy”.

mistakes.tr: I speak English. / I'm speaking English.
mistakes.why: There's no “am” before a French verb: {{je parle}} is both “I speak” and “I'm speaking”.
{{Je}} becomes {{j'}} before a vowel or a silent {{h}}.
“They” takes {{-ent}}, and it's silent. {{-ons}} goes with {{nous}}.

lessons.title: Say what you like and don't like
lessons.summary: Say what you love, like and can't stand, and what you like doing: {{aimer}} with {{le, la, les}}, and with a verb.
lessons.topic: {{aimer, adorer, détester, préférer}} + {{le, la, les}} for things in general; + infinitive; {{aimer bien}}

goal.t: J'adore le chocolat, mais je déteste le café.
goal.tr: I love chocolate, but I hate coffee.

dialog.t: Tu aimes le cinéma ?
dialog.tr: Do you like movies?

dialog.t: Oui, j'adore les films français. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: Yes, I love French movies. And you?

dialog.t: J'aime bien, mais je préfère le théâtre.
dialog.tr: I like them, but I prefer the theater.

dialog.t: Ah bon ? Moi, je n'aime pas beaucoup le théâtre…
dialog.tr: Really? I don't much like the theater…

dialog.t: Tu aimes danser ?
dialog.tr: Do you like dancing?

dialog.t: Oui, j'adore danser !
dialog.tr: Yes, I love dancing!

blocks.p: **Things in general take “the”.** In English you like “coffee”, “cats”, “French movies”, with no article. French needs one, and when you mean a thing in general (coffee as such, cats as a whole), it's {{le, la, les}}: {{J'aime le café.}} {{J'adore les chats.}}
**Aimer bien is a little less than aimer.** With things, the two are close. With a person, careful: {{je t'aime}} is “I love you”, but {{je t'aime bien}} is only “I like you”.

**Liking doing something: + infinitive.** Put the second verb in its basic form: {{J'aime danser.}} “I like dancing.” {{Je déteste attendre.}} “I hate waiting.” Where English has “-ing”, French has the infinitive.
**No de here.** After {{ne … pas}}, {{le, la, les}} stay as they are (only {{un, une, des}} become {{de}}): {{Je n'aime pas le café.}}
**Préférer** changes its accent when the ending is silent: {{je préfère}}, {{tu préfères}}, {{il préfère}}, {{ils préfèrent}}, but {{nous préférons}}, {{vous préférez}}.

ex.t: Je préfère la mer à la montagne.
ex.tr: I prefer the sea to the mountains.

ex.t: Je n'aime pas travailler le dimanche.
ex.tr: I don't like working on Sundays.

blocks.tip: To agree: {{Moi aussi.}} “Me too.” To agree with a negative: {{Moi non plus.}} “Me neither.” To disagree: {{Pas moi !}} after a yes, {{Moi, si !}} after a no.

mistakes.why: French needs an article, and a thing in general takes {{le, la, les}}.
Only {{un, une, des}} become {{de}} after a negative. {{Le, la, les}} stay.

lessons.title: Order food and drink
lessons.summary: Order a meal, ask for water, say you don't eat meat: {{du, de la, des}} for “some”, with {{prendre}} and {{boire}}.
lessons.topic: the partitive {{du, de la, de l', des}}; {{pas de}}; {{prendre}}, {{boire}}

goal.t: Pour moi, du poulet avec des frites, et de l'eau, s'il vous plaît.
goal.tr: For me, chicken with fries, and some water, please.

dialog.t: Vous avez choisi ?
dialog.tr: Have you decided?

dialog.t: Oui. Je prends le poulet avec des frites.
dialog.tr: Yes. I'll have the chicken with fries.

dialog.t: Et comme boisson ?
dialog.tr: And to drink?

dialog.t: De l'eau, s'il vous plaît. Une carafe d'eau.
dialog.tr: Water, please. A jug of tap water.

dialog.t: Moi, je ne mange pas de viande. Il y a un plat végétarien ?
dialog.tr: I don't eat meat. Is there a vegetarian dish?

dialog.t: Oui, des lasagnes aux légumes.
dialog.tr: Yes, vegetable lasagna.

blocks.p: **Some: du, de la.** English often says nothing (“I'd like water”) or “some” (“Do you want some bread?”). French always needs an article. For an amount of something you don't count, like bread, water or cheese, it's {{du}} or {{de la}}: {{du pain}} “(some) bread”, {{de la confiture}} “(some) jam”.

blocks.means: the article for “some of” a thing: {{du}}, {{de la}}, {{de l'}}, and {{des}} for several things. It means an amount of it, not all of it and not one.

blocks.p: **Three articles, three meanings.** {{J'aime le fromage.}} “I like cheese” (in general: lesson 14). {{Je voudrais un fromage.}} “I'd like a cheese” (one whole cheese). {{Je mange du fromage.}} “I'm eating cheese” (some of it).
**After a negative: de.** Like {{un}} and {{une}}, {{du, de la, des}} become {{de}} (or {{d'}}) after a negative: {{Je ne mange pas de viande.}} “I don't eat meat.”

**Ordering: je prends.** In a café or a restaurant the French say {{je prends…}} “I'll have…” (word for word “I take”) or {{pour moi…}} “for me…”, as well as {{je voudrais}}. {{Prendre}} “to take, to have” and {{boire}} “to drink” are irregular:

ex.t: Je prends un café et un croissant.
ex.tr: I'll have a coffee and a croissant.

ex.t: Elle boit du thé le matin.
ex.tr: She drinks tea in the morning.

ex.t: Il y a de la soupe ce soir.

blocks.tip: Tap water is free in a French restaurant: ask for {{une carafe d'eau}}. And {{manger}} keeps an {{e}} before {{-ons}}, so the {{g}} stays soft: {{nous mangeons}}.

mistakes.why: French needs an article: “some water” is {{de l'eau}}.

mistakes.wrong: Je ne mange pas du poisson.
mistakes.right: Je ne mange pas de poisson.
mistakes.why: After a negative, {{du}} becomes {{de}}.
With {{aimer}}, you mean cheese in general: {{le}}.

lessons.title: Say where you're going and where you're from
lessons.summary: Say you're going to the market, to France or to a friend's place, or coming back from work: {{aller}} and {{venir}}, with {{au}}, {{en}} and {{chez}}.
lessons.topic: {{aller}}, {{venir}}; {{à}} and {{de}} with places; {{en France}}, {{au Canada}}, {{aux États-Unis}}; {{chez}}

goal.t: Je vais au marché, puis chez ma grand-mère.
goal.tr: I'm going to the market, then to my grandmother's.

dialog.t: Bonjour ! Vous allez où ?
dialog.tr: Hello! Where are you going?

dialog.t: Je vais à la poste, puis au supermarché. Et vous ?
dialog.tr: I'm going to the post office, then to the supermarket. And you?

dialog.t: Je viens du marché. Et ce week-end, je vais chez ma fille, à Nantes.
dialog.tr: I'm coming from the market. And this weekend I'm going to my daughter's, in Nantes.

dialog.t: Bon week-end !
dialog.tr: Have a nice weekend!

blocks.p: **Aller and venir.** “To go” and “to come” are irregular, and among the most useful verbs in French:

**To a place: à.** “To” is {{à}}, and it joins with {{le}} and {{les}} as in lesson 11: {{je vais au cinéma}}, {{à la plage}}, {{à l'hôtel}}, {{aux toilettes}}. Before a city, just {{à}}: {{je vais à Paris}}.
**From a place: de.** “From” is {{de}}, which joins the same way: {{je viens du bureau}}, {{de la plage}}, {{de Paris}}. It's also how you say where you come from: {{Je viens de Chicago.}}

**Countries.** Feminine countries (most of those ending in {{-e}}) take {{en}}: {{en France}}, {{en Italie}}, {{en Espagne}}. Masculine ones take {{au}}: {{au Canada}}, {{au Japon}}, {{au Mexique}}. Plural ones take {{aux}}: {{aux États-Unis}}. The same word means “to” and “in”: {{Je vais en France.}} {{J'habite en France.}}

**To someone's place: chez.** {{Chez}} means “at the home of” or “to the home of”: {{chez ma grand-mère}}, {{chez Paul}}, {{chez moi}} “at my place, home”. Also for some professionals: {{chez le médecin}} “to the doctor's”.

ex.t: Tu vas où ? — Je vais au travail.
ex.tr: Where are you going? — I'm going to work.

ex.t: On va à la plage cet après-midi ?
ex.tr: Shall we go to the beach this afternoon?

ex.t: Nous allons en Italie en août.
ex.tr: We're going to Italy in August.

blocks.tip: {{Aller}} is also how the French ask how you are (lesson 2): {{Comment allez-vous ?}}, word for word “How are you going?”.

mistakes.why: {{À}} + {{le}} is always {{au}}.
A feminine country takes {{en}}.
To a person's home: {{chez}}.

practice.tr: Tonight I'm going to the movies.
They're going to Japan in May.

options: Je vais chez Marc. Tu viens ?

lessons.title: Talk about your free time and the weather
lessons.summary: Say what you do on weekends, the sports and music you play, and what the weather's like: {{faire}}, {{jouer à}} and {{jouer de}}.
lessons.topic: {{faire}}; {{faire du sport}}, {{faire les courses}}; {{jouer au foot}}, {{jouer du piano}}; {{il fait beau}}, {{il pleut}}

goal.t: Le samedi, je fais du vélo, et le dimanche, je joue au tennis.
goal.tr: On Saturdays I go cycling, and on Sundays I play tennis.

dialog.t: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
dialog.tr: What are you doing this weekend?

dialog.t: S'il fait beau, je fais une randonnée.
dialog.tr: If it's nice out, I'm going hiking.

dialog.t: Et s'il pleut ?
dialog.tr: And if it rains?

dialog.t: Je joue du piano et je fais le ménage !
dialog.tr: I play the piano and do the cleaning!

dialog.t: Moi, je joue au foot avec des amis. Tu viens ?
dialog.tr: I'm playing soccer with some friends. Are you coming?

blocks.p: **Faire: “do” and “make”.** {{Faire}} is everywhere in French: it covers both “do” and “make”, and a lot of activities. Its {{vous}} and {{ils}} forms are irregular: {{vous faites}} (never “faisez”), {{ils font}}.

**Sports and hobbies: faire du, de la.** They take {{faire}} and the partitive of lesson 15: {{faire du sport}}, {{du vélo}} (cycling), {{du yoga}}, {{de la natation}} (swimming), {{de la musique}}. Chores take {{faire}} with {{le, la, les}}: {{faire la cuisine}} (cook), {{faire le ménage}} (clean), {{faire les courses}} (do the grocery shopping).

**Playing: jouer à, jouer de.** A game or a sport: {{jouer à}}, joined to the article: {{jouer au foot}}, {{jouer aux cartes}}. A musical instrument: {{jouer de}}: {{jouer du piano}}, {{jouer de la guitare}}.

**The weather: il fait.** {{Il fait beau.}} “It's nice out.” {{Il fait chaud.}} “It's hot.” {{Il fait froid.}} “It's cold.” Rain and snow have their own verbs: {{il pleut}} “it's raining”, {{il neige}} “it's snowing”. To ask: {{Quel temps fait-il ?}} “What's the weather like?”

ex.t: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce soir ?
Je fais du yoga le matin.
ex.tr: I do yoga in the morning.

ex.t: Mon frère joue de la guitare.
Nous faisons les courses le samedi.
ex.tr: We do the grocery shopping on Saturdays.

ex.t: Il pleut, on reste à la maison.

blocks.tip: {{Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?}} can mean “What are you doing?” or “What do you do?”. To ask about someone's job, the French say {{Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?}}, “What do you do in life?”.

mistakes.why: {{Faire}} is irregular: {{vous faites}}.
An instrument takes {{jouer de}}, and {{de}} + {{le}} = {{du}}.
The weather takes {{il fait}}.

practice.tr: On Sundays we go cycling.
She plays tennis.
Do you play the guitar?

practice.q: It's sunny and warm. You say…
practice.why: The weather takes {{il fait}}. ({{Il est beau}} means “He's good-looking”!)

lessons.title: Say when and how often
lessons.summary: Tell the time, say on which days and how often you do things, and what you never do: {{à huit heures}}, {{le lundi}}, {{souvent}}, {{ne … jamais}}.
lessons.topic: the time ({{il est … heures}}); {{lundi}} or {{le lundi}}; {{toujours, souvent, parfois}}; {{ne … jamais}}

goal.t: Le lundi, je commence à huit heures, mais je ne travaille jamais le week-end.
goal.tr: On Mondays I start at eight, but I never work on weekends.

dialog.t: Vous êtes libre quand ?
dialog.tr: When are you free?

dialog.t: Le mardi et le jeudi, après dix-sept heures.
dialog.tr: On Tuesdays and Thursdays, after 5 p.m.

dialog.t: Jeudi à dix-huit heures, ça va ?
dialog.tr: Thursday at 6 p.m., is that OK?

dialog.t: Oui, parfait. À jeudi !
dialog.tr: Yes, perfect. See you Thursday!

blocks.p: **The time.** {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} “What time is it?” The answer is {{il est}}, the number and {{heures}}: {{Il est huit heures.}} The minutes come straight after: {{Il est huit heures dix.}} “It's 8:10.”

table: {{neuf heures moins le quart}} (nine less the quarter)

blocks.p: **The 24-hour clock.** Timetables, shops and appointments use it: {{dix-huit heures}} “6 p.m.”, {{vingt heures trente}} “8:30 p.m.”, written {{18 h}}, {{20 h 30}}. “At” a time is {{à}}: {{à huit heures}}.

**Days.** {{lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche}}, with small letters. One particular day takes no article: {{jeudi}} “on Thursday”. Every week takes {{le}}: {{le jeudi}} “on Thursdays”. The parts of the day work the same way: {{le matin}} “in the morning, every morning”, {{le soir}} “in the evening”.

blocks.means: a word that says how, when or how often: often, well, very, never.

blocks.p: **How often.** {{Toujours}} (always), {{souvent}} (often), {{parfois}} (sometimes) and {{rarement}} (rarely) go right after the verb: {{Je mange souvent au restaurant.}} “I often eat out.”

**Never: ne … jamais.** “Never” works like {{ne … pas}} (lesson 6), with {{jamais}} in place of {{pas}}: {{Je ne travaille jamais le dimanche.}} And like {{pas}}, it turns {{un, du, des}} into {{de}}: {{Il ne boit jamais de café.}}

ex.t: Il est dix heures et demie.
Le train part à quinze heures vingt.
Je fais les courses le samedi matin.
ex.tr: I do the grocery shopping on Saturday mornings.
Shall we have dinner together on Friday?
She often goes to the movies.

ex.t: Je ne mange jamais de viande.

blocks.tip: {{Quelle heure est-il ?}} is the textbook question. In the street you'll mostly hear {{Il est quelle heure ?}} or {{Vous avez l'heure ?}} “Do you have the time?”.

mistakes.why: No preposition before a day: {{lundi}}, or {{le lundi}} for every Monday.

mistakes.wrong: Je ne jamais travaille le dimanche.
mistakes.right: Je ne travaille jamais le dimanche.
mistakes.why: The verb goes between {{ne}} and {{jamais}}.
The word {{heures}} is always said.

lessons.title: Say what you're going to do
lessons.summary: Talk about your plans for tonight, the weekend or next year: {{aller}} + an infinitive, the everyday future.
lessons.topic: {{aller}} + infinitive (the near future); {{ce soir, demain, la semaine prochaine}}; {{je ne vais pas…}}

goal.t: Demain, je vais visiter le Louvre avec mes parents.
goal.tr: Tomorrow I'm going to visit the Louvre with my parents.

dialog.t: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire pendant les vacances ?
dialog.tr: What are you going to do during the vacation?

dialog.t: Je vais aller en Bretagne. On va faire du camping !
dialog.tr: I'm going to go to Brittany. We're going to go camping!

dialog.t: Super ! Vous allez rester combien de temps ?
dialog.tr: Great! How long are you going to stay?

dialog.t: Une semaine. Et toi ?
dialog.tr: A week. And you?

dialog.t: Moi, je ne vais pas partir. Je vais travailler…
dialog.tr: I'm not going away. I'm going to work…

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: the present, a past, a future.

blocks.p: **Going to do: aller + infinitive.** Exactly like English “I'm going to…”: {{aller}} in the present (lesson 16), then the second verb in the infinitive. {{Je vais regarder}} “I'm going to watch”.

It's for plans and for what's about to happen, as in English, and in speech it's the usual way to talk about the future: {{Il va pleuvoir.}} “It's going to rain.” (Lesson 38 has the other future, the one-word one.)
**Not going to: ne … pas around aller.** {{Je ne vais pas travailler demain.}} “I'm not going to work tomorrow.” The infinitive stays outside.
**When.** {{ce soir}} (tonight), {{demain}} (tomorrow), {{ce week-end}}, {{la semaine prochaine}} (next week), {{l'année prochaine}} (next year), {{bientôt}} (soon).

ex.tr: I'm going to call my mother.

ex.t: Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce week-end ?
ex.tr: What are you going to do this weekend?

ex.t: On va manger au restaurant ce soir.
ex.tr: We're going to eat out tonight.
It's going to rain this afternoon.
We're going to move next year.

ex.t: Je ne vais pas sortir ce soir, je suis fatiguée.
ex.tr: I'm not going to go out tonight, I'm tired.

blocks.tip: Two meanings of {{je vais}}: {{Je vais à la plage.}} “I'm going to the beach” (a place: {{à}}). {{Je vais nager.}} “I'm going to swim” (a verb: the infinitive, with nothing before it).

mistakes.why: Before a verb, no {{à}}: the infinitive comes straight after {{aller}}.
After {{aller}}, the second verb is the infinitive ({{-er}}).

mistakes.tr: I'm not going to go out.
mistakes.why: {{Ne … pas}} goes around {{aller}}.

practice.tr: Tomorrow we're going to visit the museum.

practice.tr: I'm not going to work tomorrow.

lessons.title: Invite, accept and say no nicely
lessons.summary: Ask someone out, ask for help, say yes with pleasure or no politely: {{vouloir}} and {{pouvoir}} + infinitive.
lessons.topic: {{vouloir}}, {{pouvoir}} + infinitive; {{Tu veux … ?}}, {{Tu peux … ?}}; {{je veux bien}}; {{je ne peux pas}}

goal.t: Tu veux venir au cinéma ce soir ? — Je veux bien, mais je ne peux pas, je travaille.
goal.tr: Do you want to come to the movies tonight? — I'd love to, but I can't, I'm working.

dialog.t: Allô, Clara ? Tu veux dîner avec moi samedi ?
dialog.tr: Hello, Clara? Do you want to have dinner with me on Saturday?

dialog.t: Samedi, je ne peux pas, je vais chez mes parents. Mais dimanche, je veux bien !
dialog.tr: Saturday I can't, I'm going to my parents'. But Sunday, I'd love to!

dialog.t: Super ! On peut aller au restaurant italien ?
dialog.tr: Great! Can we go to the Italian restaurant?

dialog.t: Bonne idée. Tu peux réserver ?
dialog.tr: Good idea. Can you book a table?

dialog.t: Oui, pas de problème.
dialog.tr: Yes, no problem.

blocks.p: **Wanting and being able.** {{Vouloir}} “to want” and {{pouvoir}} “can, to be able to” are irregular, and both take a second verb in the infinitive: {{Je veux partir.}} “I want to leave.” {{Je peux venir.}} “I can come.”

**Inviting.** {{Tu veux venir ?}} “Do you want to come?” is how friends invite each other; with {{vous}}, {{Vous voulez venir ?}}. {{On peut … ?}} suggests something: {{On peut aller au parc ?}} “Can we go to the park?”
**Asking for help.** {{Tu peux m'aider ?}} “Can you help me?” {{Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?}} “Could you say that again, please?” ({{M'}} “me” goes before the verb: lesson 32 explains.)
**Saying yes.** {{Oui, je veux bien !}} “Yes, I'd love to!” (not “I want well”). {{Avec plaisir !}} “With pleasure!” {{D'accord.}} “OK.”

**Saying no nicely.** {{Désolé, je ne peux pas.}} “Sorry, I can't.” Then a reason ({{je travaille}}, {{je suis occupé}} “I'm busy”) and maybe {{Une autre fois ?}} “Another time?” A bare {{je ne veux pas}} sounds blunt: “I don't want to.”

ex.t: Je ne peux pas venir demain.
Vous pouvez parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?
ex.tr: Could you speak more slowly, please?

blocks.tip: {{Je veux}} is fine for what you want to do ({{Je veux apprendre le français.}}). To ask for a thing, {{je voudrais}} (lesson 3) is the polite form of this same verb: lesson 40 shows how it's made.

mistakes.why: The infinitive comes straight after {{pouvoir}}: no {{à}}.

mistakes.wrong: Tu veux venir ? — Oui, je veux.
mistakes.right: Tu veux venir ? — Oui, je veux bien !
mistakes.tr: Do you want to come? — Yes, I'd love to!
mistakes.why: A bare {{je veux}} sounds strange here. Say {{je veux bien}} or {{avec plaisir}}.
{{Ne … pas}} goes around {{pouvoir}}; the infinitive comes after.

practice.tr: Could you repeat that, please?
practice.why: Asking someone to do something: {{pouvoir}}, with {{vous}}: {{vous pouvez}}.

practice.tr: They want to visit the castle.

lessons.title: Say what you have to do and what you need
lessons.summary: Say you have to leave, that you need a doctor, that your head hurts: {{devoir}}, {{il faut}}, {{avoir besoin de}} and {{avoir mal à}}.
lessons.topic: {{devoir}} + infinitive; {{il faut}} + infinitive; {{avoir besoin de}}; {{avoir mal à}}

goal.t: J'ai mal à la tête, je dois rentrer à la maison.
goal.tr: I have a headache, I have to go home.

dialog.t: Bonjour, madame. Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?
dialog.tr: Hello, madam. What's wrong?

dialog.t: J'ai mal à la gorge et j'ai de la fièvre.
dialog.tr: I have a sore throat and a fever.

dialog.t: Vous avez besoin de repos. Il faut boire beaucoup d'eau.
dialog.tr: You need rest. You need to drink a lot of water.

dialog.t: Je dois aller chez le médecin ?
dialog.tr: Do I have to go to the doctor?

dialog.t: Si la fièvre ne baisse pas, oui. Et vous devez prendre une pastille trois fois par jour.
dialog.tr: If the fever doesn't go down, yes. And you have to take a lozenge three times a day.

blocks.p: **Having to: devoir + infinitive.** {{Devoir}} “must, to have to” works like {{pouvoir}} (lesson 20): {{Je dois partir.}} “I have to go.”

**It's necessary: il faut.** {{Il faut}} + infinitive says what has to be done without saying by whom: {{Il faut réserver.}} “You have to book.” It never changes: there's only {{il faut}}. With a noun it means “you need, it takes”: {{Il faut deux heures.}} “It takes two hours.”
**Needing: avoir besoin de.** “I need” is “I have need of”: {{J'ai besoin d'un médecin.}} “I need a doctor.” {{J'ai besoin de dormir.}} “I need to sleep.”

**It hurts: avoir mal à.** “My head hurts” is “I have pain at the head”: {{J'ai mal à la tête.}} {{À}} joins the article as usual: {{j'ai mal au dos}} (back), {{au ventre}} (stomach), {{à la gorge}} (throat), {{aux dents}} (teeth). French says “the head”, not “my head”.

ex.tr: You have to try this restaurant!

ex.t: Il faut changer de train à Lyon.
ex.tr: You have to change trains in Lyon.

blocks.tip: {{Il ne faut pas}} means “you must not”, not “you don't have to”. For “you don't have to”, say {{tu n'es pas obligé de…}}: {{Tu n'es pas obligé de venir.}} “You don't have to come.”

mistakes.why: {{Avoir besoin}} always takes {{de}}.
With parts of the body, French says “the”, not “my”.
The infinitive comes right after {{devoir}}: no {{à}}.

lessons.title: Give directions and instructions
lessons.summary: Tell someone the way, follow a recipe, say “come in” and “don't worry”: the imperative, for {{tu}}, {{vous}} and {{nous}}.
lessons.topic: the imperative ({{prends, prenez, prenons}}); the negative imperative; {{sois, soyez}}

goal.t: Prenez la première rue à gauche, puis continuez tout droit.
goal.tr: Take the first street on the left, then keep going straight.

dialog.t: Pardon, madame, pour aller au musée, s'il vous plaît ?

blocks.means: the form of a verb that tells someone to do something: Come! Take the bus. Don't worry.

blocks.p: **Telling someone what to do.** The French imperative is the present tense without its subject: {{vous prenez}} “you take” → {{Prenez !}} “Take!” There are three: for {{tu}}, for {{vous}}, and for {{nous}}, which means “let's”.
**-er verbs lose their -s with tu.** {{Tu tournes}} → {{Tourne !}}, {{tu regardes}} → {{Regarde !}} “Look!” Other verbs keep it: {{Prends !}} {{Viens !}} {{Fais !}}
**Don't: ne … pas around it.** {{Ne prenez pas le bus.}} “Don't take the bus.” {{Ne t'inquiète pas.}} “Don't worry.” (to a friend)
**Être and avoir have their own.** {{Sois}}, {{soyez}} “be”; {{aie}}, {{ayez}} “have”: {{Soyez prudents !}} “Be careful!” {{N'ayez pas peur.}} “Don't be afraid.”

**Directions.** {{à gauche}} (on the left), {{à droite}} (on the right), {{tout droit}} (straight ahead), {{la première rue}} (the first street), {{la deuxième}} (the second), {{jusqu'au feu}} (as far as the traffic lights).

ex.t: Tournez à droite après la banque.

ex.note: a verb with {{vous}} twice: lesson 29 explains

ex.t: Coupez les tomates et ajoutez du sel.
ex.tr: Cut the tomatoes and add some salt.

blocks.tip: An imperative alone can sound bossy. Soften it with {{s'il vous plaît}}, or ask instead: {{Vous pouvez fermer la porte ?}} (lesson 20).

mistakes.why: With {{tu}}, -er verbs drop their {{-s}} in the imperative.
{{Ne … pas}} goes around the verb, as always.
{{Être}} has its own imperative: {{sois}}, {{soyez}}.

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: Tell someone what you did yesterday or last week: the passé composé, made with {{avoir}} and a past participle.
lessons.topic: the passé composé with {{avoir}}: {{j'ai parlé}}, {{j'ai fini}}, {{j'ai attendu}}; {{je n'ai pas…}}; {{hier}}, {{la semaine dernière}}

goal.t: Hier soir, j'ai dîné avec des amis et nous avons beaucoup parlé.
goal.tr: Last night I had dinner with friends and we talked a lot.

dialog.t: Tu as passé un bon week-end ?
dialog.tr: Did you have a good weekend?

dialog.t: Oui ! Samedi, j'ai travaillé dans le jardin, et dimanche, j'ai regardé le match.
dialog.tr: Yes! On Saturday I worked in the garden, and on Sunday I watched the game.

dialog.t: Ah, tu as aimé ?
dialog.tr: Oh, did you like it?

dialog.t: Non, on a perdu !
dialog.tr: No, we lost!

dialog.t: Moi, je n'ai pas regardé. J'ai fini mon livre.
dialog.tr: I didn't watch. I finished my book.

blocks.means: the form of a verb used to build a past tense, like English “talked”, “finished”, “waited”: {{parlé}}, {{fini}}, {{attendu}}.
a helper verb used to build a tense, like “have” in “I have talked”. French has two: {{avoir}} and {{être}}.

blocks.p: **The everyday past.** To say what you did, French uses the passé composé: {{avoir}} in the present (lesson 5) + a past participle. {{J'ai mangé}} is word for word “I have eaten”, but it also means “I ate”: it's the usual past when you speak.

**Making the participle.** For regular verbs, change the infinitive's ending: -er verbs end in {{-é}}, most -ir verbs in {{-i}}, -re verbs in {{-u}}. {{Parlé}} sounds just like {{parler}}: you hear the past in {{j'ai}}, {{tu as}}, {{il a}}.

**The negative goes around the helper.** {{Ne … pas}} goes around {{avoir}}, not around the participle: {{Je n'ai pas mangé.}} “I didn't eat.” Short adverbs go in the same place: {{J'ai bien dormi.}} “I slept well.” {{Nous avons beaucoup parlé.}}

**When.** {{hier}} (yesterday), {{hier soir}} (last night), {{avant-hier}} (the day before yesterday), {{la semaine dernière}} (last week), {{l'année dernière}} (last year), {{ce matin}} (this morning).

ex.t: Elle a choisi le menu à vingt euros.
Ils ont vendu leur maison l'année dernière.
ex.tr: They sold their house last year.

blocks.tip: The passé composé covers English “I ate”, “I've eaten” and “I did eat”: {{Tu as mangé ?}} is “Did you eat?” or “Have you eaten?”. One French form, three English ones.

mistakes.why: The past needs its helper: {{j'ai}} + {{mangé}}.
{{Ne … pas}} goes around the helper {{avoir}}.
-re verbs make their participle in {{-u}}: {{attendu}}.

practice.t: Hier, nous ___ travaillé jusqu'à vingt heures.
practice.tr: Yesterday we worked until 8 p.m.
Did you like the movie?

lessons.title: Tell someone about your weekend
lessons.summary: Say what you saw, did, took and drank: the irregular past participles you'll use every day.
lessons.topic: irregular past participles: {{fait, pris, vu, eu, été, bu, lu, dit, écrit, mis, ouvert, pu, voulu, dû}}

goal.t: Samedi, j'ai fait une balade, et dimanche, j'ai vu un film génial.
goal.tr: On Saturday I went for a walk, and on Sunday I saw a great movie.

dialog.t: Alors, ce week-end ?
dialog.tr: So, how was the weekend?

dialog.t: Super ! J'ai pris le train pour Bordeaux et j'ai vu des amis.
dialog.tr: Great! I took the train to Bordeaux and saw some friends.

dialog.t: Qu'est-ce que vous avez fait ?
dialog.tr: What did you do?

dialog.t: On a bu du très bon vin et on a fait du vélo.
dialog.tr: We drank some very good wine and went cycling.

dialog.t: Tu as eu de la chance ! Moi, j'ai eu un rhume…
dialog.tr: You were lucky! I had a cold…

dialog.t: Oh non ! Ça va mieux ?
dialog.tr: Oh no! Are you feeling better?

blocks.p: **The common verbs are irregular.** Most of the verbs you use every day have a participle to learn. The good news: it's a short list, and it's the same for every person: {{j'ai fait}}, {{tu as fait}}, {{ils ont fait}}.

**Patterns that help.** Verbs built on {{prendre}} share its participle: {{apprendre}} → {{appris}} (learned), {{comprendre}} → {{compris}} (understood). And {{avoir}} and {{être}} both use {{avoir}} as their helper: {{j'ai eu}} “I had”, {{j'ai été}} “I was, I've been”.

**Faire for lots of things.** {{J'ai fait une balade}} (went for a walk), {{j'ai fait du sport}}, {{j'ai fait la fête}} (partied), {{j'ai fait la grasse matinée}} (slept in). All of lesson 17's {{faire}} now has a past.

ex.note: word for word “I made the fat morning”

ex.t: J'ai mis une heure pour venir.
ex.tr: It took me an hour to get here.
ex.note: {{mettre}} + a length of time: to take

blocks.tip: {{Je n'ai pas compris.}} “I didn't understand” is one of the most useful sentences you can learn. Follow it with {{Vous pouvez répéter ?}} (lesson 20).

mistakes.why: {{Prendre}} is irregular: {{pris}}.
{{Faire}} is irregular: {{fait}}.
After {{avoir}} comes the participle ({{vu}}), not the infinitive.

lessons.title: Say where you went and when you came back
lessons.summary: Say you went to Paris, arrived late, stayed at home or were born in 1990: the verbs that make their past with {{être}}.
lessons.topic: the passé composé with {{être}} ({{je suis allé}}, {{elle est partie}}); the participle agrees with the subject

goal.t: L'été dernier, je suis allée en Italie et je suis restée deux semaines.
goal.tr: Last summer I went to Italy and I stayed for two weeks.

dialog.t: Vous êtes allés où pendant les vacances ?
dialog.tr: Where did you go on vacation?

dialog.t: Nous sommes allés en Grèce. Nous sommes partis le premier juillet.
dialog.tr: We went to Greece. We left on July first.

dialog.t: Et vous êtes rentrés quand ?
dialog.tr: And when did you get back?

dialog.t: Mon mari est rentré le quinze, mais moi, je suis restée une semaine de plus.
dialog.tr: My husband came back on the fifteenth, but I stayed a week longer.

dialog.t: Tu as de la chance !
dialog.tr: You're lucky!

blocks.p: **Some verbs use être.** About fifteen verbs, most of them about moving from one place to another or changing state, make their passé composé with {{être}} instead of {{avoir}}: {{je suis allé}} “I went”, never “j'ai allé”.

**The participle agrees with the subject.** With {{être}}, the participle behaves like an adjective (lesson 9): add {{-e}} for a woman, {{-s}} for several people, {{-es}} for several women. Usually you can't hear it ({{allé}}, {{allée}} and {{allés}} sound the same), but you write it.
**With on.** {{On}} meaning “we” takes {{est}}, and the participle usually agrees with the people meant: {{On est partis à six heures.}} “We left at six.”
**Born: je suis né.** “I was born” is {{je suis né}} (a woman writes {{je suis née}}): {{Je suis née en 1995.}}

ex.t: Nous sommes restés à la maison.
Ils sont venus à notre mariage.
Mon grand-père est né à Marseille.
ex.tr: My grandfather was born in Marseille.

blocks.tip: Most of these verbs tell a life's journey: you're born ({{naître}}), you arrive ({{arriver}}), go in ({{entrer}}), go up ({{monter}}), stay ({{rester}}), come down ({{descendre}}), go out ({{sortir}}), leave ({{partir}}), and one day you die ({{mourir}}).

mistakes.why: {{Aller}} makes its past with {{être}}.
With {{être}}, the participle agrees: {{-e}} for a woman.
Several people: {{-s}}.

practice.why: {{Partir}} is a verb of movement: {{je suis parti}}.

lessons.title: Ask someone about their trip
lessons.summary: Ask what someone did and where they went, and whether they've ever been to Paris: questions in the past, with {{déjà}}, {{pas encore}} and {{jamais}}.
lessons.topic: questions in the passé composé; {{déjà}}; {{ne … pas encore}}, {{ne … jamais}}

goal.t: Tu es déjà allé au Japon ? — Non, pas encore !
goal.tr: Have you ever been to Japan? — No, not yet!

dialog.t: Alors, ce voyage au Maroc ?
dialog.tr: So, how was the trip to Morocco?

dialog.t: Génial ! Tu es déjà allée au Maroc ?
dialog.tr: Awesome! Have you ever been to Morocco?

dialog.t: Non, jamais. Qu'est-ce que vous avez visité ?
dialog.tr: No, never. What did you visit?

dialog.t: On a visité Marrakech et on est allés dans le désert.
dialog.tr: We visited Marrakech and went into the desert.

dialog.t: Vous avez dormi sous une tente ?
dialog.tr: Did you sleep in a tent?

dialog.t: Oui ! Et j'ai mangé un couscous incroyable.
dialog.tr: Yes! And I ate an incredible couscous.

blocks.p: **Asking in the past.** The three ways of lesson 7 work in the past too. Raise your voice: {{Tu as bien dormi ?}} Put {{est-ce que}} in front: {{Est-ce que tu as bien dormi ?}} Or use a question word, first or last: {{Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ?}} {{Tu es allé où ?}}
**In formal French, inversion.** The pronoun goes after the helper, with a dash: {{Avez-vous bien dormi ?}} {{Où êtes-vous allés ?}} You'll hear it at a hotel desk.

**Ever: déjà.** {{Tu as déjà mangé des escargots ?}} “Have you ever eaten snails?” {{Déjà}} also means “already”: {{J'ai déjà mangé.}} “I've already eaten.” It goes between the helper and the participle.

**Not yet, never.** Two more negatives that work like {{ne … pas}}: {{ne … pas encore}} “not yet” and {{ne … jamais}} “never” (lesson 18). They go around the helper: {{Je n'ai pas encore fini.}} “I haven't finished yet.” {{Je ne suis jamais allé en Asie.}} “I've never been to Asia.” Short answers: {{Oui, déjà.}} {{Non, pas encore.}} {{Non, jamais.}}

ex.tr: Did you have a good vacation?

ex.t: Je n'ai jamais vu la mer.

ex.tr: Did you have a good trip?

ex.t: Tu es rentrée à quelle heure ?

blocks.tip: To show interest, react: {{Ah bon ?}} “Really?”, {{C'est vrai ?}} “Is that true?”, {{Génial !}} “Awesome!”, {{Quelle chance !}} “How lucky!”

{{Déjà}} goes between the helper and the participle.
It's {{pas encore}}, in that order, around the helper.

lessons.title: Describe how things were and used to be
lessons.summary: Describe the past and say what you used to do: {{c'était}}, {{il y avait}}, {{quand j'étais petit…}}: the imparfait.
lessons.topic: the imparfait: the {{nous}} stem + {{-ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient}}; {{être}} → {{ét-}}; for descriptions and habits

goal.t: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à la campagne et je jouais dehors tous les jours.
goal.tr: When I was little, I lived in the country and I played outside every day.

dialog.t: C'est toi, sur la photo ?
dialog.tr: Is that you in the photo?

dialog.t: Oui ! J'avais dix ans. On habitait à Lille.
dialog.tr: Yes! I was ten. We lived in Lille.

dialog.t: C'était comment ?
dialog.tr: What was it like?

dialog.t: Il faisait froid, mais c'était joli. Il n'y avait pas de télé, alors on jouait dans la rue.
dialog.tr: It was cold, but it was pretty. There was no TV, so we played in the street.

dialog.t: Et tu allais à l'école à pied ?
dialog.tr: And did you walk to school?

dialog.t: Oui, tous les matins !
dialog.tr: Yes, every morning!

blocks.means: a past tense for how things were (descriptions, feelings, the background) and for what used to happen again and again: “I was ten”, “we used to play”.

blocks.p: **Two pasts.** The passé composé (lessons 23 to 25) says what happened: an event, finished. The imparfait describes: what things were like, what was going on, what used to happen. English says “was”, “was …-ing” or “used to” for it.
**How it's made.** Take the {{nous}} form of the present ({{nous parlons}}, {{nous faisons}}), drop {{-ons}}, and add the endings. This works for every verb except {{être}}, whose stem is {{ét-}}.
As in the present, most endings sound the same: {{parlais}}, {{parlait}} and {{parlaient}} are all “par-lay”.
**Three you'll use all the time.** {{C'était}} “it was” ({{C'était super !}}), {{il y avait}} “there was, there were”, and {{il faisait}} for the weather ({{Il faisait beau.}}).

**Habits: what used to happen.** With words like {{tous les jours}} (every day), {{souvent}}, {{le dimanche}} or {{quand j'étais petit}}, the imparfait means “used to”: {{Le dimanche, on mangeait chez ma grand-mère.}} “On Sundays we used to eat at my grandmother's.”

ex.t: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
ex.tr: There were a lot of people.

ex.t: J'étais fatigué, alors je suis rentré.
ex.tr: I was tired, so I went home.
ex.note: the imparfait describes; the passé composé says what happened

ex.t: Quand nous étions jeunes, nous sortions tous les soirs.
ex.tr: When we were young, we went out every night.

ex.t: Il faisait chaud et le ciel était bleu.
ex.tr: It was hot and the sky was blue.

blocks.tip: {{Avant}} “before, in the past” + the imparfait is the easy way to say “used to”: {{Avant, j'habitais à New York.}} “I used to live in New York.”

mistakes.wrong: Quand j'ai été petit, j'ai habité à la campagne.
mistakes.right: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à la campagne.
mistakes.tr: When I was little, I lived in the country.
mistakes.why: A description, and a situation that went on for years: the imparfait.
{{C'est}} in the past is {{c'était}}: {{c'}} + {{était}}.

mistakes.wrong: Il y était beaucoup de monde.
mistakes.right: Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
mistakes.tr: There were a lot of people.
mistakes.why: {{Il y a}} comes from {{avoir}}: in the imparfait, {{il y avait}}.

lessons.title: Tell a short story
lessons.summary: Tell what happened, with its scene and its events: the imparfait for the background, the passé composé for what happened.
lessons.topic: passé composé or imparfait: the scene ({{il pleuvait}}, {{je dormais}}) and the events ({{le téléphone a sonné}})

blocks.p: **A story has a scene and events.** In English, “was …-ing” sets the scene and the simple past moves the story on. French does the same with its two pasts.

table: the background, descriptions, what was going on
what happened, one step at a time
What was it like? What was going on?

blocks.p: **An action cut short.** Something in progress (the imparfait) is interrupted by something that happens (the passé composé): {{Je prenais ma douche quand le téléphone a sonné.}} “I was taking a shower when the phone rang.”

**Words that move the story on.** {{Tout à coup}} and {{soudain}} (suddenly), {{puis}} and {{ensuite}} (then), {{alors}} (so) usually come with the passé composé. {{Pendant que}} (while), {{d'habitude}} (usually) and {{tous les jours}} go with the imparfait.

**The same verb, two meanings.** {{J'étais malade}} describes the situation: “I was ill”. {{J'ai été malade}} sums up an episode that's over: “I was ill (for a while)”. {{Il y avait du monde}} sets the scene; {{il y a eu un accident}} “there was an accident” is an event.

ex.tr: It was raining, so we stayed home.

ex.note: two things going on: both in the imparfait

ex.t: Je marchais dans la rue quand j'ai vu un vieil ami.
ex.tr: I was walking down the street when I saw an old friend.

ex.t: Quand je suis arrivé, tout le monde dansait.
ex.tr: When I arrived, everyone was dancing.

ex.t: Elle était fatiguée, mais elle a fini son travail.
ex.tr: She was tired, but she finished her work.

ex.t: Soudain, il y a eu un grand bruit.
ex.tr: Suddenly there was a loud noise.

blocks.tip: A rule of thumb: if English could say “was …-ing” or “used to”, it's the imparfait. If it's “and then…”, a single step in the story, it's the passé composé.

blocks.means: a verb with an extra little pronoun that points back to the subject: {{je me lave}}, “I wash myself”. The dictionary lists it with {{se}}: {{se laver}}.

blocks.p: **Doing it to yourself.** {{Laver}} is “to wash” (the car, a child); {{se laver}} is “to wash yourself”, “to wash”. French uses verbs like this for the whole daily routine, where English simply says “I get up”, “I get dressed”.
Before a vowel or a silent {{h}}, {{me, te, se}} become {{m', t', s'}}: {{je m'habille}}, {{il s'appelle}}. Now you know what {{je m'appelle}} (lesson 1) really is: “I call myself”.
**The negative** goes around the pronoun and the verb together: {{Je ne me lève pas.}} {{Il ne se rase jamais.}} “He never shaves.”
**Before an infinitive**, the pronoun still matches the person: {{Je vais me coucher.}} “I'm going to bed.” {{Tu dois te reposer.}} “You must rest.”

**In the imperative**, the pronoun goes after, with a dash, and {{te}} becomes {{toi}}: {{Dépêche-toi !}} “Hurry up!” {{Asseyez-vous.}} “Sit down.” (lesson 22). In the negative it stays in front: {{Ne te couche pas tard.}}

blocks.p: **Always être.** In the passé composé, every reflexive verb takes {{être}}, and the little pronoun stays in front of it: {{je me suis levé}} “I got up”.

table: {{je me suis levé}}, {{je me suis levée}}

blocks.p: **Agreement, as with the être verbs** (lesson 25): {{-e}} for a woman, {{-s}} for several. {{Elle s'est réveillée tard.}} {{Ils se sont mariés en 2010.}} “They got married in 2010.”
**The negative** goes around the pronoun and {{être}}: {{Je ne me suis pas réveillé.}} “I didn't wake up.”

**Useful ones.** {{s'amuser}} (have fun), {{se perdre}} (get lost), {{se tromper}} (make a mistake), {{se marier}} (get married), {{se rencontrer}} (meet each other), {{se passer}} (happen): {{Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ?}} “What happened?” (lesson 28).

lessons.topic: direct object pronouns {{le, la, l', les}} (and {{me, te, nous, vous}}): before the verb, before an infinitive, before the helper

goal.t: Ce pull ? Je l'ai acheté hier, et je l'adore !

dialog.t: Vous aimez cette robe ?

blocks.means: the person or thing the verb acts on directly, with no little word in between: I see **the bus**; I love **her**.

blocks.p: **Le, la, les replace a noun.** Instead of repeating “the dress”, French uses a pronoun: {{le}} for a masculine noun, {{la}} for a feminine one, {{l'}} before a vowel, {{les}} for a plural. They look like the articles, but here they mean “him, her, it, them”.

**Before the verb.** This is the big difference from English: the pronoun goes **before** the verb. “I take it” is {{je le prends}}, word for word “I it take”. In the negative, {{ne}} comes before the pronoun: {{Je ne la connais pas.}} “I don't know her.”
**With an infinitive**, it goes before the infinitive: {{Je peux l'essayer ?}} “Can I try it on?” {{Je vais les acheter.}} “I'm going to buy them.”

**In the passé composé**, before the helper: {{Je l'ai acheté.}} “I bought it.” {{Je ne l'ai pas vu.}} “I didn't see it.” (In writing, the participle agrees with a feminine or plural pronoun in front of it: {{La robe ? Je l'ai achetée.}} You usually can't hear it.)

blocks.means: the person who receives something or is spoken to, after “to”: I give a present **to my mother**; I talk **to him**. In French it comes after {{à}}.

blocks.p: **To him, to her: lui.** A person after {{à}} becomes {{lui}} (“to him” or “to her”: the same word) or {{leur}} (“to them”). Like {{le, la, les}}, they go before the verb.

**Which verbs?** The ones that take {{à}} + a person: {{parler à}} (talk to), {{téléphoner à}} (call), {{écrire à}} (write to), {{répondre à}} (answer), {{donner à}} (give), {{offrir à}} (give as a present), {{demander à}} (ask), {{dire à}} (tell). Some don't match English: “to call someone” is {{téléphoner à quelqu'un}}, word for word “to phone to someone”. So it's {{je lui téléphone}}, never “je le téléphone”.

**Same places as le, la, les.** Before the verb: {{Je ne lui parle pas.}} Before an infinitive: {{Je vais leur écrire.}} Before the helper: {{Je lui ai donné mon numéro.}} ({{Lui}} and {{leur}} never change the participle.)
**Leur or leurs?** Before a verb, {{leur}} means “to them” and never takes {{-s}}: {{je leur parle}}. Before a noun it means “their” (lesson 10): {{leur maison}}, {{leurs enfants}}.

Tu peux me passer le sel ?

lessons.summary: Answer “Are you going to Paris?” with “Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow”, and “How many?” with “I'll take two”: the little words {{y}} and {{en}}.
lessons.topic: {{y}} (there) and {{en}} (some, of it, of them); {{il y en a}}; {{on y va}}

goal.t: Des baguettes ? J'en voudrais deux, s'il vous plaît.
goal.tr: Baguettes? I'd like two, please.

blocks.p: **Y: there.** {{Y}} replaces a place that comes after {{à}}, {{en}}, {{dans}}, {{chez}}…: {{Tu vas à Paris ? — Oui, j'y vais demain.}} “Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.” French needs it: “je vais demain” on its own sounds unfinished.

**En: some, any, of it, of them.** {{En}} replaces a noun with {{du, de la, des}} or {{de}}: {{Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux.}} “Yes, I'd like some.” With a number or an amount, the number stays at the end: {{J'en voudrais deux.}} “I'd like two (of them).” {{Il en a beaucoup.}} “He has a lot (of them).”

table: {{Je n'en ai pas.}} “I don't have any.”

blocks.p: **Where they go.** Like the other pronouns: before the verb, the infinitive or the helper. {{Je n'y vais pas.}} {{Je vais en acheter.}} {{J'y suis allé l'année dernière.}} {{Tu en as mangé ?}}

**Phrases you'll hear every day.** {{Il y en a.}} “There are some.” {{Il n'y en a plus.}} “There's none left.” {{On y va !}} “Let's go!” {{Vas-y !}} “Go on! Go for it!” {{Je m'en vais.}} “I'm leaving.” And {{il y a}} itself has {{y}} in it.

lessons.title: Give reasons and link your ideas
lessons.summary: Say why, say so, and say what for: {{parce que}}, {{car}}, {{comme}}, {{donc}}, {{alors}}, {{mais}} and {{pour}} + infinitive.
lessons.topic: {{parce que}}, {{car}}, {{comme}}; {{donc}}, {{alors}}; {{mais}}, {{pourtant}}; {{pour}} + infinitive

goal.t: Je ne viens pas ce soir parce que je suis malade, mais on peut se voir demain.
goal.tr: I'm not coming tonight because I'm sick, but we can meet tomorrow.

dialog.t: Pourquoi tu apprends le français ?
dialog.tr: Why are you learning French?

dialog.t: Parce que ma copine est française, et je veux parler avec sa famille.
dialog.tr: Because my girlfriend is French, and I want to talk with her family.

dialog.t: C'est difficile ?
dialog.tr: Is it hard?

dialog.t: Un peu, mais j'adore ça. Alors, j'étudie tous les jours.
dialog.tr: A bit, but I love it. So I study every day.

dialog.t: Et tu vas en France pour la voir ?
dialog.tr: And are you going to France to see her?

dialog.t: Oui, cet été. Comme les billets sont chers, j'économise !
dialog.tr: Yes, this summer. Since the tickets are expensive, I'm saving up!

blocks.p: **Why? Because.** {{Pourquoi … ?}} “Why?”, and {{parce que}} “because”: {{Pourquoi tu pars ? — Parce que je suis fatigué.}} Before a vowel it's {{parce qu'}}: {{parce qu'il pleut}}.

table: {{Le magasin est fermé, car c'est dimanche.}}
{{Il fait beau, pourtant il fait froid.}}

blocks.p: **Comme comes first.** {{Comme}} gives the reason at the start of the sentence, often a reason the listener can see: {{Comme tu es là, on peut commencer.}} “Since you're here, we can start.” {{Parce que}} comes after the main idea.

**Donc and alors.** Both mean “so”. {{Alors}} is the more spoken one; it also starts a question or a story: {{Alors, ce voyage ?}} (lesson 26). {{Donc}} is a little more logical: {{Je pense, donc je suis.}} “I think, therefore I am.”

**What for: pour + infinitive.** A purpose, “(in order) to”, is {{pour}} + the infinitive: {{J'économise pour acheter une voiture.}} “I'm saving to buy a car.” English often just says “to”; French needs {{pour}}.

ex.t: Pourquoi tu ris ? — Parce que c'est drôle !
ex.tr: Why are you laughing? — Because it's funny!

ex.t: Je suis en retard car le train est en panne.
ex.tr: I'm late because the train has broken down.

ex.t: Comme il fait beau, on mange dehors.
ex.tr: Since it's nice out, we're eating outside.

ex.t: J'ai faim, alors je vais faire un sandwich.
ex.tr: I'm hungry, so I'm going to make a sandwich.

ex.t: C'est cher, mais c'est très bon.
ex.tr: It's expensive, but it's really good.

ex.t: Je vais à la poste pour envoyer un colis.
ex.tr: I'm going to the post office to send a package.

blocks.tip: {{À cause de}} “because of” is followed by a noun: {{à cause de la pluie}} “because of the rain”. For a good reason, say {{grâce à}} “thanks to”: {{grâce à toi}} “thanks to you”.

mistakes.wrong: Je reste ici parce que il pleut.
mistakes.right: Je reste ici parce qu'il pleut.
mistakes.tr: I'm staying here because it's raining.
mistakes.why: Before a vowel, {{parce que}} becomes {{parce qu'}}.

mistakes.tr: I'm saving to buy a car.
mistakes.why: A purpose, “in order to”: {{pour}} + infinitive.

lessons.title: Compare things and choose the best
lessons.summary: Say that one thing is bigger, cheaper or better than another, and which is the best: {{plus … que}}, {{meilleur}}, {{le plus}}.
lessons.topic: {{plus / moins / aussi … que}}; {{meilleur}}, {{mieux}}; {{le plus}}, {{le moins}}, {{le meilleur}}

goal.t: Ce restaurant est plus cher, mais il est meilleur que l'autre.
goal.tr: This restaurant is more expensive, but it's better than the other one.

dialog.t: On prend quel hôtel ?
dialog.tr: Which hotel shall we take?

dialog.t: L'hôtel du Port est moins cher que l'hôtel Bellevue.
dialog.tr: The Hôtel du Port is cheaper than the Hôtel Bellevue.

dialog.t: Oui, mais le Bellevue est plus près de la plage.
dialog.tr: Yes, but the Bellevue is closer to the beach.

dialog.t: Et les chambres sont plus grandes. C'est le meilleur hôtel de la ville !
dialog.tr: And the rooms are bigger. It's the best hotel in town!

dialog.t: Bon, d'accord. On prend le Bellevue !
dialog.tr: OK, fine. We'll take the Bellevue!

blocks.means: the form that compares two things: bigger, more expensive, better.
the form that picks out the top one: the biggest, the most expensive, the best.

blocks.p: **More, less, as.** French doesn't add an ending like “-er”: it puts {{plus}} (more), {{moins}} (less) or {{aussi}} (as) before the adjective, and {{que}} (than, as) after it.

table: {{Le train est moins cher que l'avion.}}
The train is cheaper than the plane.
{{Marie est aussi grande que sa mère.}}
Marie is as tall as her mother.

blocks.p: The adjective still agrees (lesson 9): {{Les chambres sont plus grandes.}} {{Que}} becomes {{qu'}} before a vowel: {{plus âgé qu'elle}} “older than her”. After {{que}}, “me”, “him” are {{moi}}, {{lui}}: {{Il est plus grand que moi.}}

**Good and well: meilleur, mieux.** “Better” is never “plus bon”: it's {{meilleur}}, an adjective that agrees ({{meilleure}}, {{meilleurs}}). For “well”, “better” is {{mieux}}: {{Il chante mieux que moi.}} “He sings better than me.” {{Ça va mieux.}} “I'm feeling better.”

**The most: le plus.** Put {{le}}, {{la}} or {{les}} before {{plus}} or {{moins}}: {{C'est la ville la plus chère.}} “It's the most expensive town.” “The best” is {{le meilleur}}, {{la meilleure}}. After a superlative, “in” is {{de}}: {{le meilleur restaurant de Paris}}.
**Amounts: plus de, moins de, autant de** + a noun: {{Il y a plus de monde aujourd'hui.}} “There are more people today.”

ex.t: Mon frère est plus jeune que moi.
ex.tr: My brother is younger than me.

ex.t: Le thé est aussi bon que le café.
ex.tr: Tea is as good as coffee.

ex.t: C'est la meilleure pizza du monde !
ex.tr: It's the best pizza in the world!

ex.t: Elle parle mieux français que moi.
ex.tr: She speaks French better than me.

ex.t: C'est le plus beau jour de ma vie.
ex.tr: It's the most beautiful day of my life.
ex.note: {{beau}} goes before the noun, so {{le plus beau}} does too

ex.tr: I have less time than before.

blocks.tip: {{Plus}} is said “plu” before a consonant, “pluz” before a vowel ({{plus âgé}}), and “pluss” when it means “more” on its own: {{J'en veux plus.}} “I want more.”

mistakes.why: “Better” (from “good”) is {{meilleur}}, never “plus bon”.

mistakes.wrong: Il est plus grand que je.
mistakes.right: Il est plus grand que moi.
mistakes.why: After {{que}}: {{moi}}, {{toi}}, {{lui}}…
With a verb (singing well), “better” is {{mieux}}.

answers.t: Ma sœur cuisine mieux que moi : elle fait le meilleur gâteau du monde.
